stimulus.text:
“The Congress, whenever two thirds of both Houses shall deem it necessary, shall propose Amendments to this Constitution, or, on the Application of the Legislatures of two thirds of the several States, shall call a Convention for proposing Amendments, which, in either Case, shall be valid to all Intents and Purposes, as Part of this Constitution, when ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several States, or by Conventions in three fourths thereof, as the one or the other Mode of Ratification may be proposed by the Congress. . . . no State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.”

—Constitution of the United States, Article V, September 17, 1787
stimulus.source_note: Constitution of the United States, Article V, September 17, 1787. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Constitution of the United States, Article V, September 17, 1787, public domain.

primary_sources: Constitution of the United States, Article V (September 17, 1787)

stem: According to the passage, which of the following is a way an amendment to the Constitution can be proposed?

options.text: By a majority vote of the House of Representatives alone
options.misconception: The passage requires two-thirds of both houses, not a majority of one house.

options.text: By two-thirds of both houses of Congress or by a state-called convention
By the president, with the agreement of the Supreme Court
options.misconception: The passage gives the president and the Court no role in proposing amendments.

options.text: By a majority of the states voting in a national referendum
options.misconception: The passage provides no national referendum; it provides Congress, a convention, and ratification by the states.

rationales.B: The passage names both routes: two-thirds of both houses of Congress, or a convention called when two-thirds of the state legislatures apply.
rationales.A: The passage requires two-thirds of both houses, not a majority of the House alone.
rationales.C: The passage gives neither the president nor the Court a part in proposing amendments.
rationales.D: The passage sets out proposal by Congress or convention, not a national referendum.
rationales.general:
1. Article V offers two routes for proposing an amendment.
2. The first is a vote of two-thirds of both houses of Congress.
3. The second is a convention called when the legislatures of two-thirds of the states apply.
4. The president, the Court, and a national referendum appear in neither route.
Remember: amendments are proposed by Congress or by a convention, never by one house or one official.
